front: What two elements does every crime require (plus causation for result crimes)?
back: A voluntary act (or legally required omission) — actus reus — and a culpable mental state — mens rea — that concur; result crimes also need actual and proximate causation.

front: Is a movement during an epileptic seizure a voluntary act? Can the driver still be liable?
back: No, the seizure is involuntary. But liability can rest on the prior voluntary act of choosing to drive while knowing of the risk (Decina).

front: When is a failure to act (omission) criminal?
back: Only if there is a legal duty to act (statute, contract, special relationship, voluntary assumption of care, creation of peril), the defendant knew the facts creating the duty, and could reasonably act.

front: List the common-law specific-intent crimes.
back: Solicitation, conspiracy, attempt; first-degree premeditated murder; assault (attempted battery); larceny, robbery, burglary, embezzlement, false pretenses, forgery.

front: Why does the specific/general intent distinction matter?
back: Voluntary intoxication and any honest (even unreasonable) mistake of fact can negate specific intent; for general intent, only a reasonable mistake works and voluntary intoxication is no defense.

front: Define the four MPC culpability levels.
back: Purposely: conscious object. Knowingly: aware / practically certain. Recklessly: consciously disregards a substantial and unjustifiable risk. Negligently: should be aware of such a risk. Reckless and negligent = gross deviation.

front: Under the MPC, what mental state applies if the statute is silent? If it names one mental state without specifying elements?
back: Silent: at least recklessness (§ 2.02(3)). One stated term: applies to all material elements unless a contrary purpose plainly appears (§ 2.02(4)).

front: When do courts find strict liability?
back: Public-welfare (regulatory) offenses with light penalties, plus traditional exceptions (statutory rape, bigamy). For common-law-derived or serious crimes, courts presume mens rea (Morissette; Staples).

front: Does transferred intent create attempt liability against the unintended victim?
back: No. D who shoots at A and kills B is guilty of murder of B (intent transfers) and attempted murder of A; there is no attempted murder of B.

front: Mistake of fact: what kind of mistake is a defense for (a) specific intent, (b) general intent, (c) strict liability crimes?
back: (a) Any honest mistake, even unreasonable. (b) Only an honest and reasonable mistake. (c) None.

front: When is mistake of law a defense?
back: Generally never, except (1) it negates a mental element (claim of right; Cheek willfulness), (2) reasonable reliance on an official statement of law (statute, court decision, official interpretation) later invalidated, or (3) the law was not reasonably available (Lambert). Not reliance on a private lawyer.

front: Does ordinary medical negligence break the chain of causation?
back: No. It is a foreseeable, dependent intervening cause. Only an unforeseeable, independent cause (a new attacker, an act of God, gross maltreatment as sole cause) breaks the chain.

front: When may a state prosecute a crime committed partly outside it?
back: If any element (conduct or result) occurred in the state, or conduct outside was intended to and did produce harm inside (Strassheim); MPC § 1.03.

front: State the M'Naghten test.
back: Because of a disease of the mind, at the time of the act the defendant did not know the nature and quality of the act, or did not know it was wrong.

front: State the MPC insanity test.
back: As a result of mental disease or defect, the defendant lacked substantial capacity either to appreciate the criminality (wrongfulness) of his conduct or to conform his conduct to the requirements of law (§ 4.01).

front: Federal insanity test and burden?
back: Severe mental disease or defect making the defendant unable to appreciate the nature and quality or wrongfulness of his acts; defendant proves by clear and convincing evidence (18 U.S.C. § 17).

front: Insanity vs. competency to stand trial?
back: Insanity = mental state at the time of the crime (a defense). Competency = present ability to consult with counsel rationally and understand the proceedings (Dusky); trying an incompetent defendant violates due process.

front: Is voluntary intoxication a defense to second-degree murder or battery?
back: No. Voluntary intoxication negates only specific intent; murder (malice), battery (general intent) and reckless crimes are unaffected.

front: When is involuntary intoxication a defense?
back: For any crime, if (unknowing ingestion, duress, unexpected reaction to prescribed medication) it produced incapacity meeting the insanity test or negated a required mental state.

front: California: what may voluntary intoxication negate?
back: Only actual formation of a specific intent, or for murder premeditation, deliberation or express malice — never implied malice (Pen. Code § 29.4).

front: Common-law infancy presumptions?
back: Under 7: conclusively incapable. 7–14: rebuttably presumed incapable. 14+: adult.

front: When may a person use deadly force in self-defense?
back: When he reasonably believes he faces imminent death or serious bodily injury (MPC adds kidnapping and forcible rape), the force is necessary, and he is not the initial aggressor.

front: Duty to retreat: majority vs. minority/MPC?
back: Majority: no duty to retreat. Minority and MPC: before using deadly force, retreat if you know you can do so in complete safety — except from your own home. Never a duty before non-deadly force.

front: How does an initial aggressor regain the right of self-defense?
back: By withdrawing in good faith and communicating it, or when the victim suddenly escalates non-deadly aggression to deadly force and the aggressor cannot safely withdraw.

front: What is imperfect self-defense?
back: An honest but unreasonable belief in the need for deadly force: no complete defense, but murder is reduced to voluntary manslaughter in many jurisdictions (some extend it to aggressors; California not where D's own wrongful attack justified the response).

front: Defense of others: majority test?
back: Use force if you reasonably believe the third person would be justified in using it (MPC § 3.05). Minority alter-ego rule: defender stands in the other's shoes.

front: Can deadly force be used to protect property?
back: Never to protect property alone; no spring guns. Deadly force to prevent entry into a dwelling only if reasonably necessary to prevent a violent entry and the intruder intends a felony or attack.

front: When may police use deadly force to stop a fleeing suspect?
back: Only if necessary to prevent escape and the officer has probable cause to believe the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious physical injury (Tennessee v. Garner).

front: Elements of necessity?
back: Reasonable belief conduct necessary to avoid imminent harm; harm avoided greater than harm caused; no reasonable legal alternative; defendant did not create the danger. Not a defense to intentional killing at common law.

front: Elements of duress; is it a defense to murder?
back: Threat of imminent death or serious bodily injury to D or another, reasonable fear, a person of reasonable firmness would yield, no escape, D not at fault. Not a defense to intentional murder (majority); MPC allows it.

front: Entrapment: subjective vs. objective test?
back: Subjective (majority, federal): government inducement + defendant not predisposed. Objective (MPC, California): police conduct likely to induce a normally law-abiding person; predisposition irrelevant.

front: Is offering an opportunity to commit a crime entrapment? Is inducement by a private person?
back: No to both. Mere opportunity is not inducement, and inducement must come from the government or its agent.

front: When is consent a defense?
back: When lack of consent is an element (rape, larceny) or the harm is minor or within a lawful activity (sports, medical). Never to murder or serious bodily injury; ineffective if obtained by force or fraud in the factum.

front: Define murder and list the four malice states.
back: Unlawful killing of a human being with malice aforethought: (1) intent to kill, (2) intent to inflict serious bodily injury, (3) depraved heart (extreme reckless indifference), (4) felony murder.

front: What makes a murder first degree?
back: Willful, deliberate and premeditated (reflection, even brief), or by statutory means (poison, lying in wait, torture), or felony murder during an enumerated felony.

front: What evidence shows premeditation (Anderson categories)?
back: Planning activity, motive, and a manner of killing showing a preconceived design.

front: Elements of heat-of-passion voluntary manslaughter?
back: Adequate provocation (would make a reasonable person lose control); actually provoked; no reasonable cooling time; did not actually cool.

front: Are words alone adequate provocation?
back: Not under the majority rule. Recognized categories: serious battery, mutual combat, discovery of spousal adultery, (some) illegal arrest, assault on a close relative.

front: MPC extreme mental or emotional disturbance (EMED)?
back: Murder reduced to manslaughter if committed under EMED for which there is a reasonable explanation or excuse, judged from the actor's situation as he believed it to be (§ 210.3(1)(b)). No specific trigger or cooling rule.

front: Depraved-heart murder vs. involuntary manslaughter?
back: Depraved heart: conscious disregard of a very high risk of death. Involuntary manslaughter: criminal negligence or recklessness — a substantial and unjustifiable risk, gross deviation, less extreme or not perceived.

front: What is criminal negligence?
back: A gross deviation from the standard of care of a reasonable person, creating a substantial and unjustifiable risk of death or serious injury — more than civil negligence.

front: Felony-murder basic rule?
back: A killing during the commission or attempted commission of an inherently dangerous felony is murder, even if accidental; the felonious intent supplies malice.

front: Common-law enumerated felony-murder predicates (BARRK)?
back: Burglary, arson, robbery, rape, kidnapping.

front: What is the merger (independent felony) limitation?
back: The predicate felony must be independent of the killing; assault-type felonies (assault with a deadly weapon) merge and cannot support felony murder.

front: When does the felony end for felony-murder purposes?
back: When the felons reach a place of temporary safety; killings during immediate flight are included.

front: Agency vs. proximate-cause theory of felony murder?
back: Agency (majority): only killings by a felon or accomplice count; no liability when a victim or police officer kills. Proximate cause (minority): felons liable for foreseeable deaths caused by resisters, usually excluding a justified killing of a co-felon.

front: What is misdemeanor manslaughter?
back: An unintended killing during an unlawful act not amounting to a qualifying felony (often limited to malum in se acts or where death was foreseeable) = involuntary manslaughter.

front: California felony murder after SB 1437 (Pen. Code § 189(e))?
back: Participant liable only if (1) actual killer, (2) aided the actual killer in first-degree murder with intent to kill, or (3) major participant acting with reckless indifference to human life; malice not imputed from participation (§ 188(a)(3)).

front: Elements of larceny?
back: Trespassory taking and carrying away of tangible personal property of another with intent to permanently deprive, at the time of taking.

front: What is the continuing-trespass doctrine?
back: If D takes property wrongfully without intent to steal and later forms that intent, the trespass continues and larceny is complete. Not if the original taking was lawful.

front: Employee custody vs. possession — which crime?
back: An employee with mere custody (cashier) who takes = larceny. One with lawful possession (agent, trustee) who converts = embezzlement.

front: Is intent to repay a defense to embezzlement?
back: Intent to return the exact property is; intent to repay with equivalent money is not.

front: False pretenses vs. larceny by trick?
back: Both use fraud. False pretenses: victim passes title. Larceny by trick: victim passes only possession.

front: Elements of receiving stolen property? What if police recovered the goods first?
back: Receiving possession or control of stolen property, knowing it is stolen, intending to deprive the owner. Recovered goods are no longer stolen: no receiving, but attempted receiving under the modern rule.

front: Elements of robbery?
back: Larceny + from the person or presence + by force or intimidation (threat of immediate harm).

front: Pickpocket the victim never noticed — robbery?
back: No; no force beyond that needed to take and no intimidation. Larceny.

front: Robbery vs. extortion?
back: Robbery: threat of immediate harm, property taken from person or presence. Extortion: threat of future harm (injury, exposure, accusation).

front: Elements of common-law burglary?
back: Breaking and entering the dwelling of another at nighttime with intent to commit a felony therein (intent at entry).

front: Is walking through an open door a breaking?
back: No. Breaking requires creating or enlarging an opening by at least slight force, or constructive breaking by fraud or threat.

front: How have modern statutes (and the MPC) changed burglary?
back: No breaking, any building or structure, any time, intent to commit any felony or theft (MPC: any crime); MPC excludes premises open to the public.

front: Two forms of assault?
back: (1) Attempted battery (specific intent; victim need not be aware). (2) Intentional creation of reasonable apprehension of imminent bodily harm (victim must be aware).

front: California assault definition?
back: An unlawful attempt, coupled with a present ability, to commit a violent injury on another (Pen. Code § 240) — attempted-battery form only.

front: Battery elements and mental state?
back: Unlawful application of force causing bodily injury or offensive touching; general intent (intent, recklessness or criminal negligence suffices).

front: Fraud in the factum vs. fraud in the inducement in rape?
back: Factum (victim does not know the act is intercourse) vitiates consent: rape. Inducement (lies about love, money) generally does not.

front: Is reasonable mistake of age a defense to statutory rape?
back: Not under the majority (strict liability). MPC: defense if critical age above 10. California: yes for unlawful sexual intercourse (Hernandez), not lewd acts under 14.

front: Elements of kidnapping?
back: Unlawful confinement of a person against his will plus either movement (asportation) or concealment in a secret place.

front: Does moving a robbery victim to a back room make it kidnapping?
back: Usually not: movement merely incidental to another crime does not count unless it substantially increases the risk of harm or reduces detection.

front: Elements of common-law arson?
back: Malicious burning (charring, not scorching) of the dwelling of another. Malice includes reckless disregard; arson is not specific intent.

front: When is possession a voluntary act?
back: When the possessor knowingly procured or received the item or was aware of control long enough to end possession (MPC § 2.01(4)). Actual or constructive; mere proximity insufficient.

front: Mental state for attempt?
back: Specific intent to commit the target crime — even if the target crime requires less. No attempted involuntary manslaughter or felony murder; attempted murder needs intent to kill.

front: Dangerous proximity vs. substantial step?
back: Common law: conduct dangerously close to completion (Rizzo). MPC/modern: a substantial step strongly corroborative of criminal purpose (lying in wait, reconnoitering, possessing tools).

front: Is factual impossibility a defense to attempt? Legal impossibility?
back: Factual: never. Hybrid legal (goods not actually stolen): no defense under the modern/MPC rule — judge facts as D believed. Pure legal (act is not a crime): defense.

front: Is abandonment a defense to attempt?
back: Common law: no, once beyond preparation. MPC: complete and voluntary renunciation is an affirmative defense — not if prompted by fear of detection or postponement.

front: When is solicitation complete? Does it merge?
back: When the request is made, whether or not accepted. Merges into conspiracy (if agreement) or the completed crime.

front: Elements of conspiracy?
back: Agreement between two or more persons; intent to agree; intent to achieve the unlawful object; overt act in furtherance (most jurisdictions; not common law).

front: Bilateral vs. unilateral conspiracy — undercover agent?
back: Bilateral (common law, federal): no conspiracy if the only other party feigns agreement. Unilateral (MPC, modern majority of states): conspiracy, because D agreed.

front: When is a supplier of goods a conspirator?
back: Only with intent to further the crime, inferred from a stake in the venture: inflated prices, goods with no legitimate use, large share of business, or a serious crime (Falcone; Direct Sales; Lauria).

front: Pinkerton rule?
back: Each conspirator is liable for crimes of co-conspirators committed in furtherance of the conspiracy and reasonably foreseeable. The MPC rejects it.

front: Does conspiracy merge with the completed crime?
back: No (common law and federal); D can be convicted of both. MPC § 1.07 bars conviction of both.

front: Withdrawal from a conspiracy — effect and requirements?
back: Never a defense to the conspiracy itself once complete (common law); cuts off Pinkerton liability for later crimes if D takes an affirmative act communicated to all co-conspirators or notifies police. MPC: renunciation that thwarts success.

front: What is Wharton's rule?
back: No conspiracy where the crime necessarily requires the participation of exactly the agreeing parties (adultery, dueling, bigamy) unless more join.

front: Elements of accomplice liability?
back: Aid, counsel or encouragement + intent to aid + intent that the principal commit the crime. Mere presence is not enough.

front: For what crimes is an accomplice liable?
back: The intended crime and (common law) any other crime that was a natural and probable consequence of it. MPC: only crimes purposely aided.

front: How does an accomplice withdraw?
back: Before the crime is unstoppable: repudiate encouragement; neutralize material aid; or warn police / try to prevent the crime.

front: Elements of accessory after the fact?
back: Completed felony; knowledge of it; aid to the felon; intent to help him avoid arrest, trial or punishment. Separate, lesser crime.

front: Two tests for a Fourth Amendment search?
back: Katz: intrusion on a subjective expectation of privacy society recognizes as reasonable. Jones/Jardines: physical trespass on a person, house, paper or effect to obtain information.

front: What did Kyllo, Carpenter and Chatrie hold?
back: Kyllo: thermal imaging of a home is a search. Carpenter: historical cell-site location data requires a warrant. Chatrie (2026): accessing geofence location history is a search.

front: Name five places or things with no reasonable expectation of privacy.
back: Open fields; garbage left at the curb; areas visible from public airspace; bank records and dialed numbers (third-party doctrine); voice, handwriting and other things knowingly exposed.

front: Who has Fourth Amendment standing in another's home or car?
back: Overnight guests (Olson) and drivers in sole possession of a rental car (Byrd) do; short-term business visitors (Carter) and mere passengers (Rakas) do not — though passengers may challenge the stop (Brendlin).

front: When is a person seized?
back: When by physical force or a show of authority to which he submits, his freedom is restrained so that a reasonable person would not feel free to leave or decline. Fleeing suspect who has not submitted is not seized (Hodari D.).

front: Standard for a Terry stop? For a frisk?
back: Stop: reasonable suspicion from specific, articulable facts that criminal activity is afoot. Frisk: reasonable belief the person is armed and dangerous; pat-down for weapons only.

front: Does an anonymous tip justify a stop?
back: A bare tip with only readily observable details does not (J.L.); one with predictive details corroborated by police does (White); a contemporaneous 911 eyewitness report can (Navarette).

front: Plain-feel rule?
back: During a lawful frisk, an officer may seize an object whose contraband identity is immediately apparent by touch, without manipulating it (Dickerson).

front: Can police prolong a traffic stop for a dog sniff?
back: Not without independent reasonable suspicion; the stop may last only as long as needed for its mission (Rodriguez). The sniff itself is not a search (Caballes).

front: When do police need an arrest warrant?
back: Not for a public arrest on probable cause (Watson). They need one to enter the suspect's home (Payton), and a search warrant to enter a third party's home (Steagald), absent exigency or consent.

front: Requirements of a valid search warrant?
back: Probable cause (Gates totality), neutral and detached magistrate, oath, particular description of place and items; proper execution (knock and announce).

front: What is a Franks hearing?
back: Defendant who substantially shows the affiant deliberately or recklessly included a false statement necessary to probable cause gets a hearing; if proved, the warrant is void.

front: Scope of search incident to arrest?
back: The arrestee's person and area within immediate control (Chimel/Robinson), contemporaneous with a lawful custodial arrest.

front: Gant rule for vehicles?
back: If the arrestee is a recent occupant (Thornton), search the passenger compartment incident to arrest only if the arrestee is unsecured and within reaching distance, or it is reasonable to believe evidence of the offense of arrest is in the vehicle.

front: Can police search a cell phone's data incident to arrest?
back: No; they need a warrant (Riley), absent a true exigency.

front: Automobile exception?
back: Probable cause that a vehicle contains contraband or evidence → warrantless search of the whole vehicle and any container that could hold the item, including passengers' belongings; not in a home's curtilage (Collins).

front: Plain view requirements?
back: Lawful vantage point, lawful access, incriminating character immediately apparent (probable cause). Inadvertence not required (Horton); moving an item to inspect is a search (Hicks).

front: Must police tell a person he may refuse consent?
back: No. Voluntariness is judged by the totality; knowledge of the right to refuse is only a factor (Schneckloth).

front: Co-occupant consent rules?
back: Common or apparent authority suffices (Matlock; Rodriguez); a physically present co-occupant's express objection controls as to him (Randolph), unless he is lawfully removed (Fernandez).

front: Emergency-aid exception standard after Case v. Montana (2026)?
back: Officers may enter a home without a warrant when they have an objectively reasonable basis to believe an occupant needs immediate aid; probable cause is not required.

front: Which special-needs searches need no probable cause?
back: Inventory (standard procedures), sobriety and border checkpoints, border searches, school searches on reasonable grounds, probationer/parolee searches, closely regulated business inspections.

front: Where does the exclusionary rule not apply?
back: Grand jury, civil and parole proceedings, federal habeas (Stone v. Powell), and impeachment of the defendant's own testimony.

front: How does California's Truth-in-Evidence clause affect suppression?
back: Cal. Const. art. I, § 28(f)(2): California courts exclude evidence only where the federal Constitution requires (In re Lance W.).

front: Three exceptions to fruit of the poisonous tree?
back: Independent source (Murray), inevitable discovery (Nix), attenuation (Brown factors: time, intervening circumstances, flagrancy; Strieff).

front: Four situations where Leon good faith does not apply?
back: Bare-bones affidavit; facially deficient warrant; affiant misled the magistrate (Franks); magistrate abandoned judicial role.

front: Do knock-and-announce violations require exclusion?
back: No (Hudson v. Michigan).

front: When is a confession involuntary under due process?
back: When police coercion overbears the suspect's will under the totality of circumstances; coercive police activity is required (Connelly). Inadmissible even to impeach.

front: Miranda custody test?
back: Whether a reasonable person would feel free to end questioning and leave, and whether the setting has station-house coercive pressures; routine traffic and Terry stops are not custody.

front: Miranda interrogation test?
back: Express questioning or its functional equivalent: words or actions police should know are reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response (Innis).

front: Is an undercover cellmate's questioning Miranda interrogation?
back: No (Perkins) — no police-dominated atmosphere. But after charges it may violate the Sixth Amendment (Henry).

front: Can a Miranda waiver be implied?
back: Yes: understanding the warnings followed by an uncoerced statement is an implied waiver (Butler; Thompkins).

front: How must a suspect invoke the right to silence, and what follows?
back: Unambiguously (silence is not enough — Thompkins). Police must scrupulously honor it; resumption only after significant time, new warnings, usually a different crime (Mosley).

front: Edwards rule?
back: Once a suspect in custody unambiguously requests counsel, all interrogation about any crime stops until counsel is present, unless the suspect reinitiates; protection lapses after 14 days out of custody (Shatzer).

front: Is 'Maybe I should talk to a lawyer' an invocation?
back: No — not unambiguous (Davis); police may continue.

front: Public-safety exception?
back: Questions prompted by an immediate, objective concern for public safety may precede warnings; answers admissible (Quarles).

front: Elstad vs. Seibert?
back: Elstad: after a voluntary unwarned statement, a later warned and waived statement is admissible. Seibert (plurality; Kennedy concurrence test): not if police deliberately used question-first, warn-later without curative measures.

front: Can a Miranda-defective statement be used at trial at all?
back: Yes, to impeach the defendant's inconsistent testimony if voluntary (Harris); physical fruits are admissible (Patane, plurality).

front: What does the Fifth Amendment privilege protect?
back: Compelled, testimonial, incriminating communications. Not blood, fingerprints, voice or handwriting exemplars, or lineups (Schmerber; Wade).

front: When does the Sixth Amendment right to counsel attach, and what does Massiah forbid?
back: At formal charge, indictment, information, arraignment or first appearance. After that, police may not deliberately elicit statements about the charged offense without counsel or waiver.

front: Is the Sixth Amendment right offense-specific?
back: Yes (McNeil; Cobb uses Blockburger) — police may question about uncharged, different offenses (subject to Miranda).

front: When must counsel be appointed for an indigent?
back: Every felony; misdemeanors only if imprisonment (incl. suspended sentence) is actually imposed; first appeal as of right.

front: Requirements to represent oneself (Faretta)?
back: Timely, unequivocal request; knowing and intelligent waiver; competence. A state may insist on counsel for one too mentally ill to conduct trial (Indiana v. Edwards).

front: Strickland test?
back: Deficient performance below an objective standard of reasonableness + prejudice: reasonable probability of a different result.

front: Right to counsel at lineups and photo arrays?
back: Yes at post-charge live lineups (Wade); no at pre-charge lineups (Kirby, plurality) or photo arrays (Ash).

front: Due-process test for identifications and the Biggers factors?
back: Police-arranged procedure unnecessarily suggestive + substantial likelihood of misidentification. Reliability factors: opportunity to view, attention, accuracy of description, certainty, time elapsed.

front: Bail and pretrial detention rules?
back: Bail not higher than needed to assure appearance (Stack); preventive detention after an adversary hearing is valid (Salerno); probable-cause hearing within 48 hours (McLaughlin).

front: Barker v. Wingo speedy-trial factors?
back: Length of delay, reason for delay, defendant's assertion, prejudice. Remedy: dismissal with prejudice.

front: When is there a right to a jury trial?
back: For offenses with an authorized penalty of more than six months' imprisonment; jury of at least 6; unanimous for serious offenses (Ramos).

front: Batson three steps?
back: (1) Prima facie showing of discriminatory strike; (2) neutral explanation; (3) court decides whether purposeful discrimination is proved.

front: Apprendi rule?
back: Other than a prior conviction, any fact that increases the penalty beyond the statutory maximum (or a mandatory minimum) must be found by a jury beyond a reasonable doubt.

front: Crawford rule?
back: Testimonial hearsay of an absent witness is inadmissible unless the witness is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine.

front: Brady duty?
back: Prosecution must disclose favorable (exculpatory or impeachment) evidence that is material — reasonable probability of a different result — regardless of good faith.

front: Dusky competency standard?
back: Sufficient present ability to consult with counsel with a reasonable degree of rational understanding and a rational and factual understanding of the proceedings.

front: Requirements for a valid guilty plea?
back: Knowing, intelligent, voluntary on the record: court explains the nature of the charge, maximum penalty and rights waived, and finds a factual basis (Boykin; Rule 11).

front: When does jeopardy attach?
back: Jury trial: jury empaneled and sworn. Bench trial: first witness sworn. Plea: court accepts it.

front: Blockburger test?
back: Two offenses are the same unless each requires proof of an element the other does not; a lesser-included offense is the same as the greater (Brown v. Ohio).

front: When may a defendant be retried after a mistrial?
back: Hung jury: yes. Mistrial over objection: only for manifest necessity. Mistrial on defense motion: yes unless the prosecution goaded it (Oregon v. Kennedy).

front: Dual sovereignty doctrine?
back: State and federal governments (and two states) may each prosecute the same conduct (Gamble); a city and its state are one sovereign.

front: Death-penalty categorical bars?
back: Non-homicide crimes against individuals (Coker; Kennedy); minor felony-murder accomplices (Enmund, unless Tison major participant with reckless indifference); intellectual disability (Atkins); under 18 (Roper); insanity (Ford).

front: Status vs. conduct under the Eighth Amendment?
back: Punishing a status (addiction) is cruel and unusual (Robinson); punishing conduct is not (Powell, plurality; Grants Pass camping bans).

front: Can a state put the burden of an affirmative defense on the defendant?
back: Yes if it does not negate an element (Patterson; Martin; Leland); not if it shifts proof of an element (Mullaney). Mandatory presumptions on elements are invalid (Sandstrom).

front: Harmless error vs. structural error?
back: Most constitutional errors: harmless if the prosecution proves beyond a reasonable doubt they did not contribute (Chapman). Structural errors (denial of counsel, biased judge, defective reasonable-doubt instruction) require automatic reversal.

front: California essays: which law governs Criminal Law and Procedure?
back: General principles (common law, noting the MPC) for crimes and the U.S. Constitution for procedure, unless the call asks for California law.

front: Fourth Amendment essay order for each item of evidence?
back: Government action → standing → search/seizure? → warrant or exception → exclusionary rule and its limits → conclusion.

front: Statement-suppression essay order?
back: Voluntariness → Miranda (custody, interrogation, public safety, warnings, waiver, invocation) → Sixth Amendment (if charged) → fruit of illegal arrest → impeachment use.

front: California: can a conviction rest on an accomplice's uncorroborated testimony?
back: No (Pen. Code § 1111): other evidence must tend to connect D with the offense; proof of the crime alone is not enough. Accomplice = one liable for the identical offense. Federal/MBE: no corroboration rule.
